# hexmap

<!-- badges: start -->
[![Lifecycle: experimental](https://img.shields.io/badge/lifecycle-experimental-orange.svg)](https://lifecycle.r-lib.org/articles/stages.html#experimental)
<!-- badges: end -->

The hexmap R package converts geospatial polygons into a map of equally sized hexagons. Every region gets the same amount of ink, so small but important regions (such as inner-city electorates) are as visible as large, sparsely populated ones.

## Installation

You can install the development version of hexmap like so:

``` r
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("numbats/hexmap")
```

## Method

1. **Tile** (`hex_grid()`): choose a hexagon size so that one hexagon per region covers the same area as the map, then keep the hexagons that overlap the map the most. Landmasses that are far enough apart (such as Tasmania and the mainland) are tiled separately and kept at least one hexagon apart.
2. **Allocate** (`tile_allocate()`): give each region exactly one hexagon, minimising the total squared distance between regions and their hexagons. This optimal assignment is solved with the Hungarian algorithm. Optionally, regions can be grouped (e.g. by state) so that each group's hexagons are contiguous.

When grouping, the map is first warped with a diffusion cartogram so that each group's area matches its number of regions while keeping its shape (`layout_diffusion()`), and the borders between groups are then repaired so that groups touch as they do on the map (`layout_repair()`). Other layouts, such as compact blocks (`layout_compact()`) or a spatial treemap (`layout_slice()`), can be given to `group_layout`.

`hexmap()` does both steps in one call.

## Example: Australian federal election 2025

The `aec2025` data is an `sf` object with simplified boundaries of the 150 electoral divisions used at the 3 May 2025 Australian federal election, and the party that won each division.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(hexmap)
library(sf)
library(ggplot2)

party_colours <- c(ALP = "#D7263D", LNP = "#1F4E9C", GRN = "#2E9E44", Other = "#8C8C8C")
party_labels <- c(ALP = "Labor", LNP = "Coalition", GRN = "Greens", Other = "Independents & others")

winner_map <- function(data) {
  ggplot(data) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = winner), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = party_colours, labels = party_labels, breaks = names(party_labels), name = NULL) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
```

Labor won a large majority:

```{r results}
seats <- table(factor(aec2025$winner, levels = names(party_labels)))
data.frame(party = party_labels, seats = as.vector(seats), row.names = NULL)
```

### Choropleth map

On a geographic map the result looks like a Coalition landslide, because the large rural divisions dominate the picture while Labor's many small city seats are barely visible.

```{r plot-choropleth}
aec2025 <- st_transform(aec2025, crs = 3577)
winner_map(aec2025)
```

### Hexagon map

The hexagon map gives every division the same area, so the map shows the number of seats won by each party.

```{r plot-hexmap}
aec2025_hex <- hexmap(aec2025)
winner_map(aec2025_hex)
```

Colouring by state shows where the divisions have moved. The overall shape of Australia and the relative positions of divisions are kept, but the densely populated south-east has far more divisions than land, so Victorian and Sydney divisions spill inland. Tasmania is tiled as a separate island, with one hexagon for each of its five divisions.

```{r plot-hexmap-state}
ggplot(aec2025_hex) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = state), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  theme_void()
```

### Grouping by state

Grouping the divisions by state keeps each state's hexagons together, and a small gap along the state borders makes each state visually distinct. By default the map is warped so that each state's area is closer to its number of divisions, which enlarges the densely populated south-east while Western Australia and the Northern Territory shrink. Each state keeps its shape and touches the same states as on the map.

```{r plot-hexmap-group}
aec2025_state_hex <- hexmap(aec2025, group = state)
winner_map(aec2025_state_hex)
```

Layouts are functions, so their options can be changed. `alpha` sets how far the map is warped, from keeping the outline of Australia (`alpha = 0`) to making each state's area proportional to its number of divisions (`alpha = 1`). Other layouts can also be repaired, such as compact blocks in the style of election maps:

```{r plot-hexmap-layouts, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4}
library(patchwork)
layouts <- list(
  "layout_diffusion(alpha = 0.25)" = layout_repair(layout_diffusion(alpha = 0.25)),
  "layout_diffusion(alpha = 1)" = layout_repair(layout_diffusion(alpha = 1)),
  "layout_compact()" = layout_repair(layout_compact())
)
maps <- lapply(names(layouts), function(name) {
  ggplot(hexmap(aec2025, group = state, group_layout = layouts[[name]])) +
    geom_sf(aes(fill = state), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
    labs(title = name) +
    theme_void()
})
wrap_plots(maps)
```
